newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finns rehearse plan to cope with nuclear accident.
newsitem.headline: Finns rehearse plan to cope with nuclear accident.

text.p: What if a radiation cloud was headed your way after an accident at a nuclear plant in Finland? Hundreds of experts in Europe and beyond will join a dry-run on Thursday to test their responses, partly using the Internet.
Panic on the streets will not be a feature of the exercise -- planners say the focus will be for authorities to see how to get information out and react.
Even nuclear accidents have their jargon, and experts talk of two clear phases in Thursday's: a "threat" situation -- when a leak may happen -- and a "release" situation -- when it has.
"The release phase might be fairly long," said Leif Blomqvist, head instructor of the Finnish emergency services college and one of the event's planners.
The "accident" will happen at the Loviisa nuclear power station on the south coast of Finland, activating "alerts" in 26 other countries across Europe, and even as far as South Korea.

Any emissions will be imaginary but experts will use the real weather and forecasts to try to predict the likely course of radioactive fallout, and the action they would take if it were for real. That is where the international aspect comes in.

Weather and nuclear experts in the neighbouring Nordic countries and France, Germany, Britain and beyond will be monitoring the chances of contamination and "reacting". They can later assess whether they made the right decisions.

"If you evacuate people, you should always strive to do it in the threat phase," said Blomqvist. "If a release started very suddenly it would be best to shelter inside. But a large release would not be that instantaneous -- it would depend..."
Also built into the test is an assumption that the nuclear plant's operators may try to play down the danger -- experts have to independently assess all available information.

That might make it relevant to Japan, where prosecutors may file charges against a nuclear processing plant operator which admitted covering up the country's worst nuclear accident in March. But planners say Japan is not due to join this practice.
With the main aim being to test getting information to all the authorities that need it, and handling the mass media and the public at large, Finnish authorities face a stressful time.
A group of firefighters in the central town of Kuopio will simulate "the general public", bombarding emergency services with telephone calls. Troublemakers are not ruled out.
A special Internet site will be used to carry real-time "media" cover of the incident.

It will include real audio and text "press releases" as well as reporting by a dummy real-time news agency. Student journalists will join international reporters, playing themselves, to harass information providers.
"The Internet means we'll be able to simulate what would be put on the radio and other mass media and the authorities will have that information almost as in a real situation," Blomqvist said.

But ordinary World Wide Web surfers will not be able to see the simulated accident: the site will be password-protected to make sure it does not get overloaded and avoid a possible alarmist response, Blomqvist said.
You can read about the plan and see nuclear monitoring details at page http://www.intermin.fi/sm/pelastus.
For Blomqvist, who will be responsible for presenting the radiation situation, the challenge is considerable: "I can't plan everything because of the real weather," he said.
Forecasters said the situation so far was extremely unclear, with Finland currently between two weather fronts, but it looks like stronger winds, most probably heading south.
The exercise is part of a two-year programme put together by the Nuclear Energy Agency of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
